The problem

Nobody is short of dashboards.

Fleet operations fail in the gap between knowing and fixing. Every tool we buy sits on the knowing side of that gap.

1 Drift rots quietly

A namespace ships without a NetworkPolicy. A cluster falls off its release channel. Nothing alerts, because nothing is broken — until it is.

2 Alerts are not fixes

A page at 03:00 hands someone a symptom. A human still has to read the cluster, write the YAML, open the PR, and chase the review.

3 Review does not scale

Fleet-wide posture reviews happen quarterly because they cost an engineer a week. Between them, the fleet is unobserved.

The scarce resource is not knowledge — it is the labour between the finding and the fix.  kube-agents automates that stretch, and stops at the pull request so a human still decides.

What it is

Agents that live inside your cluster.

Not a SaaS that scrapes your fleet from outside. kube-agents runs as a Deployment in your own cluster, reads through the Kubernetes API, and writes only through Git.

K8s A Kubernetes operator

Go / Kubebuilder. Reconciles a PlatformAgent custom resource — the whole install is one declarative object you can put in Git.

Pod An agent Deployment

Runs the Hermes runtime and hosts three co-located profiles: the Chat Agent, the Platform Agent, and per-cluster Cluster Agents scaffolded on demand.

LLM An inference gateway

LiteLLM for hosted models (Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI) or vLLM for local models on GPU nodes. Model choice is yours, and swappable.

Chat Agent
The front door. Listens on Google Chat and Slack, routes work, relays progress.

Platform Agent
The specialist. Fleet-wide reads, a library of GKE skills, the GitOps write path.

Cluster Agents
One read-only profile per managed cluster, for runtime debugging in place.

Two ways to think about it

Reactive when you ask. Proactive when you don't.

Most agent products are one or the other. The value compounds when the same skills serve both.

💬 ChatOps interface

Ask in Google Chat or Slack. The Chat Agent routes the request to the Platform Agent, which runs skills, inspects clusters through the Kubernetes MCP server, and reports back in-thread.

  • “Why is checkout-prod throttling?”
  • “Onboard this app to the gitops repo”
  • “What is this cluster costing us?”

Answers in seconds No kubectl required

⏱ Proactive autonomy

Two things start work with nobody asking: the clock, pointing the Platform Agent at governance SOPs on a rolling schedule, and the cluster itself, when a warning event opens its own diagnostic session. Both end in a ledger issue and pull requests you review.

  • Runs whether or not anyone is watching
  • Cron for what should be true; events for what just broke
  • Ends at the repo, not in a chat backlog

⚙ Plumbing, not audits

Four more jobs run on the Chat Agent with no model attached at all — profile-cron-tick, cluster-agent-reconcile, and the bootstrap inventory pair. They are scheduler mechanics; they cost nothing per tick.

✓ Safety at the tick

  • Per-job locks — a slow run never doubles up
  • Prompt-injection scan on everything it reads
  • [SILENT] runs post nothing when there is nothing to say
  • Hard turn cap per run, then it stops

Five further watchdogs shipped disabled and have since been retired. The roster gets smaller as well as bigger.

The third trigger

Nobody files the ticket. The cluster does.

A warning event in any managed cluster opens its own diagnostic session. The agent is already working on the root cause before anyone has read the alert.

One failure is one incident

Session opens

Root cause in chat
Diagnosis and options, in a thread

It waits before it shouts. A crash-loop warning has to repeat three times before it counts. A startup race that clears on its own never opens a session — and never pages anyone.

A bad tag is not a bad day. ImagePullBackOff covers both. A typo will never resolve, so it fires at once; a registry rate-limit clears itself, so it is held back.

One failure, one thread. A rolling window folds every repeat into the same incident, and a daily per-severity ceiling bounds what a mass failure can post.

In practice  ·  Event-driven RCA

The alert arrives with the root cause already attached.

No dashboard to open and no kubectl to run. One thread carries the diagnosis, the options, and — once you say so — the pull request.

⚡ It starts with the evidence

The session opens holding the event itself — cluster, namespace, object, reason, repeat count — then investigates the live cluster read-only, exactly as a Cluster Agent would.

↩ The thread remembers

The triage report is stored against the chat thread, so a reply five hours later still reaches the fixer with the whole diagnosis attached. You never re-explain the incident.

✓ The fix is still a pull request

Nothing is applied to the cluster. The agent branches, edits the manifest in the GitOps repo and opens a PR — the same narrow, reviewable diff every other path produces.

One switch turns it off. eventWatcher.enabled: false on the custom resource, for the day you want silence.

Kickoff. A sentence in chat starts every audit stream at once — no console, no runbook, no ticket.

The fleet-audit feature

A report is not a change.

The single design decision the whole feature turns on: findings go to an issue, fixes go to a pull request — one narrow diff at a time.

Tier 1

The standing ledger

Each audit stream owns exactly one open GitHub issue. Every run rewrites it in full, so what you read is today's state of the fleet — never an archaeology of stale comments.

  • Comments carry only the delta — what appeared, what closed
  • A clean run closes the ledger as completed
  • No new issue per run. No inbox to triage.

Tier 2

The remediation PR

A finding with a mergeable manifest is promoted into a narrow pull request that links back to the ledger. One finding, one file, one decision.

  • Critical findings promote automatically, capped at five per run
  • Everything else on request: comment /remediate <finding-id> or /remediate all
  • Every request gets exactly one answer — a PR, or a reason why not

Why the split matters to a reviewer: you can read the whole fleet's posture in five issues, and you never review a 400-line diff to fix one namespace. Closing a PR is a decision the ledger records — the finding simply stays open.

Tier 1  ·  the ledger, in the repo

Five standing issues. That is the entire report surface.

github.com/gke-agentic/adamparco-infra/issues

Live GitOps repository, captured 4 August. Every open issue is an audit ledger, labelled by stream and severity. Nothing else accumulates here.

Labels do the filing

Every artefact the agent opens is self-describing, so a human can slice the board without reading a single body.

agent:audit audit:compliance-audit audit:remediation severity:critical severity:major

And it excludes itself

The github-issue-resolver watchdog that triages inbound issues skips anything carrying agent:audit — the agent does not review its own homework.

Tier 1  ·  inside a ledger

Scope, findings, state — rewritten every run.

github.com/gke-agentic/adamparco-infra/issues/28 — Security & RBAC Posture Audit
  • A scope table first. Which clusters were read, and how many checks completed on each. The coverage line is part of the report, not a footnote.
  • A findings table, with state. Each row carries a stable finding id, a severity, and where it lives — so the same drift keeps the same identity across runs.
  • State points at the fix. The highlighted column reads fix proposed (#34, #35, #36) — the ledger knows which pull requests answer which findings.
  • Evidence under every finding. The exact read-only command, and its verbatim output.

Because the body is rewritten rather than appended, the issue is always as long as the problem — 43 findings or zero, it reads the same way.

Tier 1  ·  what changed since last time

The comment thread is a changelog, not a pile.

issues/28 — audit delta, and the PRs it opened

New findings only. Then GitHub's own cross-reference: mentioned this in 2 pull requests — #39 and #40. The audit trail is native, not bolted on.

issues/28 — the next run, five findings resolved

And good news, reported. The run that finds the fixes merged says so — five resolved — rather than letting the improvement be the only silent outcome.

Tier 2  ·  the remediation pull request

Nine lines, one namespace, one decision.

github.com/gke-agentic/adamparco-infra/pull/39
  • Opened by a bot identity, on a branch named for the finding.
  • The body is the case for the change: where it applies, the impact, the finding id, the evidence command and its output, the recommendation, why this fix, and — unusually — the risk on apply.
  • It links back: Part of #28 ties the diff to the ledger row that justified it.
  • The diff is nine lines. A default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy. Reviewable in fifteen seconds.

Note the honesty. “Existing, undocumented cross-namespace inbound traffic will be blocked. Enumerate legitimate inbound callers first.” The agent argues against its own patch where the risk is real.

Tier 2  ·  one finding, one pull request

The second namespace gets its own PR — deliberately.

github.com/gke-agentic/adamparco-infra/pull/40
  • Same defect, different cluster. #39 fixes adamparco-gitops, #40 fixes ap-ap-deploy-test. Seven seconds apart, from the same audit run.
  • Not batched — and that is the point. Merging one namespace's policy must never be blocked by a disagreement about another's.
  • Rejecting a fix is cheap. Close the PR; the finding stays on the ledger and no replacement is opened automatically. Nothing is silently retried.

Closing the loop

Auto-merge plus ArgoCD makes it self-healing.

The pull request is the seam. Leave a human in it, or — where policy allows — take the human out and the fleet repairs itself.

Finding closes on the ledger

Compliance restored without a human — when you opt in. Detection, fix, apply and verification are all mechanised.

The rollback is a git revert. Because the change is a commit, undoing it is the thing your team already knows how to do.

Merged but still reproducing? The ledger says so explicitly — ⚠ fix merged, still reproduces — rather than quietly closing.

Finding lifecycle

Seven states, and none of them are “probably fine”.

A finding is a tracked object with an identity that survives across runs. This is the whole vocabulary.

State Means
open Reproduces. No fix proposed yet.
fix proposed A PR exists and is waiting on a human.
resolved (fix merged) The PR merged and the finding no longer reproduces.
resolved Gone, without an agent PR. Someone else fixed it.
State Means
⚠ fix merged, still reproduces The fix was wrong or incomplete. Loudly flagged.
fix refused A human closed the PR. Recorded, never re-proposed.
fix withdrawn The agent pulled its own PR; awaiting re-proposal.

“Fix refused” is the important one. A human decision to reject a change is durable state. The agent will not quietly re-open the same pull request next Monday — which is the single behaviour that makes an autonomous system tolerable to live with.

Why you can trust the output

Evidence, not assertions.

Every finding carries the exact read-only command that produced it, and its verbatim output. If it cannot be reproduced, it is dropped — not softened.

  • A finding with no reproducible command never ships. The bar is a command you can paste, not a claim you have to believe.
  • Coverage is itself evidence. The scope table reports what could not be read.
  • It prefers an honest 7/11 to a false all-clear. An audit that could not see the whole fleet leaves its ledger open and says where it went blind.
  • Secrets are redacted before anything reaches a GitHub body.
# evidence, copied verbatim into the ledger $ gcloud container clusters describe adamparco-gitops \ --location us-east4 \ --format='json(releaseChannel, currentMasterVersion)' { "currentMasterVersion": "1.35.6-gke.125", "releaseChannel": { "channel": "REGULAR" } }

Security posture

Three independent planes. Read is the default.

The agent's blast radius is not a promise in a prompt — it is what three separate permission systems will let it do.

1 Kubernetes RBAC

The in-cluster ServiceAccount is bound read-only. The agent can describe the world and change nothing in it.

read-only

2 GCP IAM

Ships with a read-only permission set. A gke-admin set exists and is strictly opt-in, per install.

read-only default admin opt-in

3 The GitOps path

The only write the agent has is a pull request, using a short-lived, repo-scoped token minted per operation by Minty.

write via review

gVisor sandbox
The agent pod runs under runtime separation.

No long-lived GitHub PAT
Tokens are minted from a KMS-signed JWT and expire.

Injection scanned
Content the agent reads is screened before it acts.

Destructive ops always ask
Cluster deletion and IAM revocation gate on a human.

Bottom line

What a reviewer is actually being offered.

An autonomous auditor that reads the fleet on a schedule, keeps exactly one standing report per stream, proves every claim with a command you can rerun, and proposes fixes one narrow diff at a time — where a human, or your branch protection, decides. The report never touches the cluster. The pull request is the only thing that can.

↓ Lower toil

Posture review stops being a quarterly project staffed by a person and becomes a daily background process with a five-issue surface.

↑ Faster remediation

Detection to reviewable fix collapses from weeks to minutes, and to seconds where auto-merge and ArgoCD are allowed to close the loop.

= Same governance

Every change is still a commit, still reviewed, still revertible. The audit trail is GitHub's, not a vendor's.

Get started

One script. One custom resource.

The working install path is GKE via the provisioning script. It bootstraps the cluster, the operator CRDs, IAM bindings, Chat ingress, secrets, and the Platform Agent itself.

$ git clone https://github.com/gke-labs/kube-agents.git $ cd kube-agents/k8s-operator/scripts $ ./provision.sh → GKE Standard cluster + operator CRDs → IAM bindings (read-only by default) → Google Chat Pub/Sub ingress → PlatformAgent CR reconciled ✓ agent pod Running — watchdogs scheduled
